message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No, the evidence doesn't support that statement, so it shouldn't go in the paper.

- **The report itself says the question is open.** No arm of the trial cut meetings without also cutting hours, so the trial can't show the hours cut was necessary.
- **The one observation you found points the other way, if anywhere.** The two control offices that audited their meetings without changing hours saw a 4.1% rise in output per hour. That is two offices with no comparison group, so it proves nothing either way. But it hints that some of the gain might be available without the hours cut. It doesn't show the cut is essential.
- **The meetings finding makes the question more pressing.** About half the measured per-hour gain ran through fewer meetings. The board will reasonably ask whether a meetings review alone would get some of that benefit at lower cost.

Here is wording the evidence does support:

> "The evidence does not establish whether reducing hours is necessary for the gain. About half of the measured per-hour improvement came through fewer recurring meetings. Two control offices that cut meetings without reducing hours saw a smaller rise (4.1%), but this was unplanned and uncontrolled. Whether reorganising work alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such changes happen and stick, remains untested."

If the paper needs a position, you can still argue that the hours cut is a reliable way to force reorganisation that might not otherwise happen. Present that as the team's judgement, not as a finding.
